name: Elena's oxygen and water on a mountain hike

parameters.label: Altitude
parameters.explain: Air pressure falls as you go up, so each breath holds less oxygen. Altitude sickness usually starts above about 8,000 feet.

parameters.label: Hiking pace
parameters.explain: Working harder means more sweat and faster breathing — and every breath out carries water away.

parameters.label: Days spent at altitude first
parameters.explain: Bodies adjust to thin air over days. Going up gradually is the most important way to avoid altitude sickness.

parameters.label: Water drunk
parameters.explain: Drinking replaces what sweat and breathing take out. In the heat, a cup every 15–20 minutes is the usual advice.

parameters.label: Hours hiking
parameters.explain: Water loss adds up hour after hour if drinking doesn't keep up.

parameters.label: Resting heart rate at home
parameters.explain: Most people rest at 60–100 beats a minute; fitter people are often lower.

parameters.label: Body weight
parameters.explain: The same water loss is a bigger share of a smaller body.

parameters.label: Air temperature
parameters.explain: Sun and warm air make you sweat more.

overlay.caption: thin air → less oxygen per breath → breathe & pump harder · sweat + dry breath → water lost

explain.summary: Elena has two problems at once. High up, the air pressure is lower, so each breath brings in less oxygen — her heart and lungs speed up even while she sits. Separately, sweating in the sun and breathing hard in dry mountain air take water out of her body faster than one small bottle can replace. Water helps the headache; only going down fixes the thin air.
rules: Air pressure — and the oxygen in each breath — falls with altitude, using NASA's standard-atmosphere formula.
Her sitting heart rate and breathing rise to make up for the missing oxygen; after a few days at altitude this extra effort shrinks.
Water lost each hour = sweat (more with pace and heat) + water breathed out (more with thinner air and faster breathing).
Body water falls by the water lost minus the water drunk, over the hours of the hike.
As body water drops, pee gets darker and scarcer and thirst switches on.

source.fact: In the lower atmosphere, temperature T (°F) = 59 − 0.00356 × altitude (ft), and pressure = 2116 × [(T + 459.7) / 518.6]^5.256 pounds per square foot.

Altitude sickness comes from lower air pressure and oxygen, usually above about 8,000 feet; a rapid pulse, shortness of breath with effort and headache are common; going up gradually is the most important prevention, and drinking plenty of fluids is advised.
Signs of dehydration include extreme thirst, urinating less, dark-coloured urine and dizziness; sweating in hot weather causes fluid loss.
For activity in the heat, drink about 1 cup of water every 15–20 minutes.
Sweat loss = drop in body weight plus fluid drunk; dividing by time gives sweat rate.
Most people's resting heart rate is 60–100 beats a minute.

choice.what: Oxygen per breath is shown as a share of sea-level air pressure
choice.why: The air is still about 21% oxygen at altitude; what drops is the pressure, so each breath holds fewer oxygen molecules.

choice.what: Sitting heart rate rises 0.75 beats for each 1% less oxygen
choice.why: Chosen so Elena goes from 70 at home to about 95 at 11,000 ft, matching the clue. Real increases vary between people.

choice.what: The extra heart and breathing effort halves every 3 days at altitude
choice.why: Bodies adjust over days to weeks; 3 days is a teaching value.

choice.what: Water breathed out grows with thinner air and faster breathing
choice.why: Each breath out carries water vapour; faster breathing in dry mountain air loses more. The amounts are estimates.

choice.what: Body water is shown as a share of the water in a body (about 60% of body weight)
choice.why: Keeps the numbers easy to compare; pee and thirst bands are teaching lines.

illustrative: Elena's weight, her half-cup an hour and the four-hour climb are made up for a fictional story.
Her sitting breathing rate and the size of the water-loss terms are estimates, not measurements.
provenance.studying: Why some people get altitude sickness much more easily than others is still being studied.

citations.title: Earth Atmosphere Model — Imperial Units
citations.supports: Troposphere equations in English units: T = 59 − 0.00356·h (°F, h in feet) and p = 2116 · [(T + 459.7)/518.6]^5.256 (pounds per square foot).

citations.title: High altitude illness
citations.supports: Caused by reduced air pressure and lower oxygen at high altitude, usually above 8,000 ft; symptoms include headache, rapid pulse and shortness of breath with exertion; gradual ascent is the most important prevention; drink plenty of fluids.

citations.title: Dehydration — Symptoms and causes
citations.supports: Lists extreme thirst, urinating less, dark-colored urine and dizziness as signs; sweating, especially in hot weather, causes fluid loss.

citations.title: Heat Stress — Workplace Recommendations
citations.supports: For moderate activity in the heat lasting under 2 hours, drink 1 cup (8 oz) of water every 15–20 minutes.

citations.title: Sweat Rate Calculator
citations.publisher: Korey Stringer Institute, University of Connecticut
citations.supports: Sweat loss equals body weight before minus after, plus fluid drunk; sweat rate is that loss divided by exercise time.

citations.title: Target Heart Rates Chart
citations.supports: A resting heart rate between 60 and 100 beats per minute is normal for most adults; athletes or very active people can be as low as 40.

does: Shows air pressure — and so oxygen per breath — falling with altitude, from a standard NASA formula
Shows the heart and lungs working harder at rest high up, and settling after days of adjusting
Shows water loss from sweat and breathing adding up over a hike, and drinking making up for it
doesnt: Measure any real person — Elena is fictional and the numbers are estimates
Model altitude sickness itself, or say who will get it
Include food, salt, wind or cold
limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: A headache, sick feeling or unusual breathlessness on a mountain is a reason to stop, drink water and tell an adult — going down is the real fix.
